title: Semiconductor Supply Chain Resilience Post-COVID
abstract: A new report from a Taipei research house argues that the chip industry's post-pandemic resilience push has quietly reshaped capital spending priorities across three continents.
body:
## Semiconductor Supply Chain Resilience Post-COVID

On 2026-05-08, the Taipei-based research house SemiVision published a 214-page assessment of how the global semiconductor supply chain has changed since the COVID-19 disruptions of 2020–2022. The report, titled *Redundant by Design*, concludes that resilience spending has become a permanent line item in the capital budgets of the world's largest chipmakers, even as the immediate memory of pandemic-era shortages fades. SemiVision analyst Lin Wei-ting, the report's lead author, told reporters that the industry has moved from just-in-time to just-in-case without fully acknowledging the cost.

## The New Geography of Wafer Capacity

The most visible change is geographic. In 2019, roughly 78 percent of leading-edge logic wafer capacity sat in Taiwan and South Korea. By the first quarter of 2026, that figure had fallen to 61 percent, according to SemiVision's tally. The shift is not because Taiwan or South Korea lost capacity; both added fabs. It is because the United States, Japan, and Germany added more. TSMC's Arizona campus now runs three fabs at volume, with a fourth under construction. Samsung's Taylor, Texas, plant began shipping 2-nanometer wafers in late 2025. Intel Foundry's Ohio complex, after two years of delays, reached risk production in March 2026.

Lin cautions that geographic diversification has not come cheap. The average cost per wafer at a new US or European fab is 38 percent higher than at an equivalent facility in Taiwan, a gap that has narrowed only slightly since 2023. "Resilience is a tax," Lin said. "The question is whether governments and customers are willing to keep paying it." So far, the answer appears to be yes. The US CHIPS and Science Act, the EU Chips Act, and Japan's semiconductor subsidy program have together committed more than 180 billion dollars in direct grants and tax credits through 2030.

## Inventory Strategy and the Memory Cycle

For memory makers, the post-COVID period brought a different lesson. During the pandemic, DRAM and NAND buyers panicked, double-ordering and driving prices to unsustainable highs. When demand collapsed in late 2022, memory firms suffered record losses. Since then, the three largest DRAM producers have adopted what SemiVision calls "structured inventory bands"—target ranges for finished goods that trigger production cuts or increases automatically. The result, according to the report, is a memory cycle that is 40 percent less volatile than the 2015–2022 average.

Not everyone is convinced. Park Ji-hoon, a senior analyst at Seoul-based Meridian Capital, argues that the new bands merely delay the next bust. "You cannot automate away the capital cycle," Park said. "When every player follows the same rule, they all cut at once, and the shortage that follows is worse." SemiVision's data shows that DRAM contract prices rose 22 percent in the first quarter of 2026, which Park cites as evidence that the bands are already failing.

## The Bank of Japan Factor

A less obvious driver of supply chain decisions has been monetary policy. The Bank of Japan's gradual exit from yield curve control, which began in 2024 and continued through 2025, raised the cost of yen-denominated borrowing for Japanese equipment makers such as Tokyo Electron and Advantest. That, in turn, pushed up the price of deposition and test tools worldwide. SemiVision estimates that BoJ policy normalization added 4 to 6 percent to the cost of a new fab toolset between 2023 and 2026.

Lin argues that this cost pressure has accelerated a shift toward used equipment and refurbishment. The global market for refurbished semiconductor tools reached 9.8 billion dollars in 2025, up from 5.1 billion in 2020. "The leading edge gets the headlines, but the trailing edge is where resilience is actually being built," Lin said. Mature-node fabs in China, Malaysia, and Vietnam have absorbed much of this refurbished capacity, reducing their dependence on new tool deliveries that can take 18 months or more.

## What Resilience Costs

The report's central finding is that resilience has a price, and that price is now embedded in chip prices. SemiVision calculates that the average selling price of a leading-edge logic wafer is 14 percent higher than it would have been under a purely efficiency-optimized supply chain. For memory, the premium is smaller, around 6 percent, because memory capacity is more fungible.

Whether customers will tolerate these premiums indefinitely is an open question. Major cloud providers, which consume a growing share of leading-edge output, have begun signing direct supply agreements that bypass traditional distributors. These agreements often include volume commitments in exchange for price ceilings, effectively transferring some resilience costs back to the chipmakers. Lin sees this as a healthy development. "The industry spent thirty years optimizing for cost," she said. "Now it is optimizing for survival. That is not a bad thing, but someone has to pay for it."

SemiVision plans to update its assessment quarterly. The next edition, due in August 2026, will include new data on packaging capacity in Southeast Asia and a detailed breakdown of subsidy disbursements by country. For now, the report's message is clear: the pandemic may be over, but the supply chain it reshaped is here to stay.
